name: Munroa

project_scope.scope: Existing canonical species only; no new admission

look_here_first: FLUFFGRASS — look at ground level, not above the prairie: a TINY (usually about 2–15 cm tall) perennial with short, wiry, sometimes sprawling/stolon-like stems ending in clustered sharp, silvery-white-edged leaves and a cottony little FLOWERING HEAD NESTLED AMONG THOSE LEAVES. Follow a stem to its leafy tip: the terminal (and sometimes axillary) head holds about 1–5 sessile or very short-stalked spikelets, each with about 6–12 fertile FLORETS. At 10–20× look for two rather equal, relatively LONG pointed GLUMES (often ~6–8 mm), and a separate 3-veined hairy lemma DEEPLY split into two lobes, with ONE stout short AWN between the lobes. The true ligule is a very short hair fringe (~0.3–0.5 mm), not a big membrane. These close-up details are NOT verifiable in the current one-photo original.

priority: Find woolly flowering clusters physically EMBEDDED within sharp pale-edged leaves at short shoot tips
Verify true 0.3–0.5 mm hair-fringe collar ligule and a 1–5-spikelet terminal fascicle
Dissect spikelet: ~6–12 florets, long paired glumes, deeply bifid hairy lemma with one notch awn
Compare raised Erioneuron pilosum heads and shallow-notched lemma, not pale color alone

comparison_lesson.title: Fluffgrass versus hairy woollygrass: leafy nest or lifted club?
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: FLUFFGRASS = woolly MULTIFLORET heads DOWN IN sharp LEAFY STARS; HAIRY WOOLLYGRASS = woolly compact clubs held UP on mostly bare STALKS. Munroa confirmation: 1–5 heads/spikelets, LONG near-equal glumes, DEEP bifid hairy lemma with ONE short awn between lobes, short hair-fringe ligule.
quick_split: HAIRY WOOLLYGRASS / Erioneuron pilosum: low perennial bunch, but SMALL TIGHT PALE CLUB HEADS are carried on LONG, mostly leafless erect stems well ABOVE the short basal leaves. FLUFFGRASS / Munroa pulchella: 1–5 compact woolly spikelets are enclosed WITHIN a whorl/cluster of sharp, sometimes nearly white leaves at the TOP of short stems, often angled down and sometimes rooting at nodes; the leafy flowering fascicle, not just woolly color, is a key distinction. Fluffgrass's two long pointed glumes are about as long as its lower spikelet and its fertile lemma is DEEPLY TWO-LOBED (about half its length) with a single stout awn between lobes. In Erioneuron pilosum the glumes are generally SHORTER than the first floret and the lemma notch is very shallow; both have hairy floral organs and hair-fringe ligules, so neither trait ALONE separates them. Other low tuft grasses and tiny Aristida can look fuzzy in drought; check the enclosed short inflorescence and individual florets under magnification. Older DASYOCHLOA PULCHELLA and ERIONEURON PULCHELLUM refer to this Munroa species, NOT the separate species Erioneuron pilosum.
comparison_lesson.guardrail: Keep Dasyochloa pulchella and Erioneuron pulchellum as historical synonyms for current Munroa pulchella. Current Erioneuron pilosum is separate. Existing county nativity/taxon review is not changed.

comparison_matrix.title: Munroa vs Erioneuron and other short dryland grasses
rows: 2–15 cm dwarf radiating perennial; cottony 1–5-spikelet panicle tucked among stiff leaves at branch tip
Hair-fringe ligule ~0.3–0.5 mm; long ~6–8 mm glumes, 6–12 florets/spikelet, 3-nerved lemma DEEPLY bifid with short single awn
Low basal tuft plus raised mostly leafless stalks with a pale dense short club at each tip
Glumes shorter than lowest fertile floret; 3-nerved hairy lemma SHALLOW notch and single tiny awn
Often more open and long-awned flowering heads; head silhouette varies
THREE awn limbs arising on one lemma, not one awn in a deep bifid lemma
Spaced hanging multi-flowered spikelets on OPEN flexuous panicle branches
Glume/lemma measurements required; not a tiny woolly cluster enclosed in terminal leaves

what_to_teach_crew: Put two WHOLE plants side by side: in Munroa the white head stays DOWN AMONG sharp leaves, in Erioneuron pilosum it is UP on slender comparatively bare stalks.
Munroa makes true small flowering heads of 1–5 SPIKELETS; a mature SPIKELET has about 6–12 FLORETS. Do not confuse these ranks.
Locate a separate true ligule hair fringe: even though both genera have hairs, the specific 0.5 mm interior fringe is not resolved by a whole-plant photograph.
For definitive ID, a Munroa fertile lemma is split conspicuously into two deep lobes framing a short awn; the Erioneuron notch is much shallower.
Recognize historical synonyms: Dasyochloa pulchella and Erioneuron pulchellum are Munroa, not additional installed genera/species.
Keep all creator/license metadata and the precise needed macro photos visible rather than claiming 'finished' from 3 non-dissected source images.
visual_needs: CONNECTED GROWTH FORM: one 2–15 cm clump with long internodes, prostrate/radiating branch tips and node rooting if present; photograph the same plant from rooted stem to leaf cluster, ruler for size.
LEAFY FASCICLE: whole head with 1–5 tucked-in woolly spikelets shorter than or equaled by immediately surrounding needlelike sharp pale-edged leaves; front and side view.
TRUE COLLAR 20×: 0.3–0.5 mm short ligule HAIR FRINGE, blade/sheath clearly opened with 1-mm ruler; do not mistake longer sheath margin hairs for ligule.
ONE MATURE SPIKELET 10–20×: note 6–12 fertile FLORETS inside ~7–13 mm compressed spikelet; scale and paired glumes visible.
GLUMES AND LEMMA: two near-equal shiny glumes reaching toward end of spikelet and 3–5 mm 3-nerved hairy fertile lemma; dissect instead of relying on pale overall fluff.
LEMMA DEEP NOTCH: two apical lobes split nearly half the lemma and ONE ~1.5–2.5 mm awn emerging from their notch, with measured mm scale.
PAIR WITH ERIONEURON: show an actual mature Erioneuron pilosum glume and shallow notched lemma (not an ordinary seedhead) at the same magnification as Munroa.
visual_status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — single physically present original target photo and 2 gross arrows, 2 additional independently source/licensed exact taxon images externally referenced, 2 real Joey Erioneuron lookalike source photos. Critical glume/lemma/ligule macros absent.

items.label: 1 · REAL FLUFFGRASS — ground-hugging leafy flowering clusters
items.image_role: Existing physically archived and manually inspected exact source-identified Munroa pulchella JPEG showing silvery starburst of stiff narrow leaves and fluffy terminal cluster. Existing 2 gross arrows retained; no microscopic organs assigned.
items.caption: Don Rideout's real taxon-labelled photograph shows the nearly ground-level starburst of stiff pale-edged leaves and white woolly tips in rocky gravel. The flowering packets are closely embraced by leaves rather than held above them on tall bare stems. This frame cannot resolve floret count, relative glume length, the true ligule or the deeply two-lobed lemma.
items.why_it_matters: Crew recognition begins by finding the WOOLLY HEAD AMONG THE TIP LEAVES. For certainty take one spikelet to 10–20×; no awn/ligule arrows here.
items.creator: Don Rideout
items.photo_status: Real pixels previously inspected and this source retested: two preexisting gross pointers retained untouched. Original Don Rideout CC BY-NC rights and all scientific holds unchanged.

items.label: 2 · ACTUAL FLUFFGRASS — close leafy spikelet clusters against sky
items.image_role: NEW externally linked genuine Munroa pulchella photo under Dasyochloa synonym, indexed by Wikimedia Commons, not yet stored as local JPG.
items.caption: Alex Abair's Commons photo (2018) shows a close-up of pale pointed leafy fascicles and compact flowering tufts held at a stem tip. This is the SAME accepted Munroa taxon under its older name Dasyochloa pulchella. It does NOT show a dissected floret: do not mistake long pointed surrounding LEAVES for lemma awns.
items.why_it_matters: Helps crew locate the woolly spikelets tucked among sharp-pointed leaves, rather than identify by generic whitish seedheads.
items.creator: Alex Abair
items.photo_status: External Wikimedia Commons 1536×2048 source photo, creator and per-file CC BY 4.0 verified; actual photo thumbnail visually inspected. Not a locally downloaded JPEG or microscopic-organ confirmation.

items.label: 3 · ACTUAL FLUFFGRASS — second licensed real-species reference
items.image_role: NEW externally linked licensed Commons exact species reference under Dasyochloa synonym; original photo not archived locally.
items.caption: Jim Morefield's photo depicts western fluffgrass (Dasyochloa/Munroa pulchella) photographed in California. This is a different source photograph from the Don Rideout and Alex Abair images, useful for seeing variation in plant habit and fluffy leafy head arrangement. Rooting, 0.5-mm ligule and dissected lemma are not confirmed from this reference.
items.why_it_matters: Compare variable field appearance while keeping the characteristic SHORT HEAD WRAPPED IN SURROUNDING LEAVES as the first clue.
items.creator: Jim Morefield
items.photo_status: External Wikimedia Commons photograph, exact source/attribution and FlickrReviewR-verified CC BY-SA 2.0; no new local binary, no annotations to uninspected micros. Original file contains GPS, but no original image file is copied to repo.

items.label: 4 · HAIRY WOOLLYGRASS — OTHER species, heads raised on bare stalks
items.image_role: Existing physically installed Joey Santore Erioneuron pilosum clump photo, DISTINCT other species used for look-alike comparison only.
items.caption: This is HAIRY WOOLLYGRASS, not fluffgrass. Notice multiple pale compact seedheads raised on mostly leafless slender stalks above a basal tuft of narrow leaves. Fluffgrass hides its flowering heads down in short leafy starbursts.
items.why_it_matters: The height and position of the head RELATIVE TO the leaf tuft is a stronger field distinction than woolly color.
items.creator: Joey Santore
items.photo_status: Physical existing Joey specimen JPEG visually inspected earlier, preserved credited use as another species. No anatomy arrows added.

items.label: 5 · HAIRY WOOLLYGRASS — OTHER species, club-shaped flowering head
items.image_role: Previously archived exact Erioneuron pilosum Joey Santore flowerhead image; DIFFERENT species comparison only.
items.caption: This is an actual Erioneuron woolly club head at close range. Compare the many overlapping pale spikelet packets at the end of a comparatively bare stalk with Munroa's leafy flowerhead. Specific glume lengths and shallow Erioneuron lemma notches remain invisible without dissection.
items.why_it_matters: Both genera have furry multi-flowered spikelets; only true glume and lemma examination securely separates close-up material.
items.creator: Joey Santore
items.photo_status: Existing actual archived photographed Erioneuron, not Munroa. Original iNaturalist CC BY-NC and source creator retained; no fabricated microscopic detail.
